source.title_on_document: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task

supplement.where: Appendices A-BC are included on PDF pp. 167-216. The reading guide points to the appendix and to https://www.brainonllm.com/ (p. 5), but identifies no separate external statistical supplement.
supplement.holds: Appendix A lists interview clusters. Appendices B-BC contain EEG connectivity figures and dDTF tables, including sums, connection counts, session patterns and significance markers. They do not supply missing arm means/SDs/SEs or treatment-effect tables for essay uniqueness or diversity.

paper_design_summary: Adults recruited from greater-Boston universities were individually randomized to ChatGPT, web search without LLMs, or no tools for supervised SAT-style essay writing; 54 people were analyzed, with 18 per original group (pp. 22-28; Table 1, p. 3). Essays received blinded teacher and AI-judge ratings and computational analyses of similarity, entities, phrasing and concepts (pp. 52-84). An optional later session reused 18 participants with tools switched; former ChatGPT users then wrote without tools, but this selected subset was not newly randomized (pp. 28, 45-46, 117).

studies.label: Supervised essay-writing experiment with optional session-4 tool switch

assignment.what_was_assigned: Initial individual assignment to ChatGPT, Search Engine or Brain-only, balanced on age and gender, retained across the initial sessions (p. 23). Returning LLM and Brain-only participants switched tools in the optional later session; participation depended on availability and no separate random assignment at follow-up is reported (pp. 28, 45 and 117).

arms.name: LLM Group (ChatGPT)
arms.description: ChatGPT was the only permitted information resource in sessions 1-3; a provided account was used, and other websites/LLMs were prohibited (pp. 23 and 27). Table 1 (p. 3) reports 18 analyzed per group. The original LLM returnee subgroup has 9 analyzed people and writes without tools in session 4 (pp. 28 and 46).

arms.name: Search Engine Group (web search; no LLM)
arms.description: Any website except LLMs; participants used Google, with "-ai" appended to queries to suppress AI-enhanced results (p. 23). Table 1 (pp. 3-4) reports 18 analyzed per group and no Search Engine session 4.

arms.name: Brain-only Group (no tools)
arms.description: No websites, online/offline tools or LLMs; participants relied on their own knowledge (pp. 23 and 27). Table 1 (p. 3) reports 18 analyzed per group. The original Brain-only returnee subgroup has 9 analyzed people and uses ChatGPT in session 4 (pp. 28, 46 and 117).

arms.name: LLM-to-Brain returnees, session 4 (no AI)
arms.description: Returning original LLM participants wrote without tools in session 4 (pp. 28, 117). The original LLM denominator is 9 on p. 46. These are members of the original 54, not an additional or independently randomized arm.

arms.name: Brain-to-LLM returnees, session 4 (ChatGPT)
arms.description: Returning original Brain-only participants used ChatGPT in session 4 (p. 117). The original Brain-only denominator is 9 on p. 46. These are members of the original 54, not an additional or independently randomized arm.

participants.exclusions: Methods report 60 recruited, 55 completing at least the initial three sessions after scheduling difficulties, and data reported only for 54 "To ensure data distribution" (p. 22). The number randomized, timing and individual selection rule for omitting a completed case, and arm-specific losses are not stated. Optional session 4 analyzed 18 of the same people, with original-group denominators of 9 LLM and 9 Brain-only (pp. 45-46, 117). The original groups each contain 18 analyzed people (p. 3, Table 1). No intention-to-treat analysis is established.
participants.who: Adults aged 18-39 recruited at MIT, Wellesley, Harvard, Tufts and Northeastern; predominantly undergraduate/postgraduate students, with university employees also described (p. 22). The education/occupation counts in the source are not fully consistent with the final analyzed total.
participants.country: United States (greater Boston, Massachusetts; pp. 1 and 22)
participants.quote: To ensure data distribution, we are here only reporting data from 54 participants (as participants were assigned in three groups, see details below).
participants.locator: p. 22, Experimental Design: Participants; p. 3, Table 1 (18 per group); pp. 45-46 and 117 (returning subset)

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI ChatGPT; participant-facing intervention model/version not stated in the saved PDF.
ai_tool.how_used: Participants used a supplied ChatGPT account during essay writing as their sole information resource; other websites and LLMs were prohibited (pp. 23, 27). Requests included drafting, structure, grammar and translation (p. 45; pp. 65-68). Researchers used llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M for analysis and judging (pp. 53, 58, 65, 68, 72); it is not identified as the participant intervention. The LLM-to-Brain returnees wrote without tools in session 4 (pp. 28, 117).

task.description: Argumentative essays on SAT-style prompts: participants chose among 3 prompts in each of sessions 1-3, for 9 offered topics overall (p. 25). Session 4 offered each returnee only topics that person had previously written about (p. 28). These outputs qualify through rated uniqueness and across-writer similarity, not solely through general essay quality.
task.duration: 20 minutes per essay (p. 27). Initial three sessions plus an optional fourth; scheduling spanned four months, but individual intersession delays are not stated (pp. 23 and 28).

outcomes.name: Essay uniqueness rated by English teachers
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two English teachers, blinded to group assignment and the existence of the groups, scored essays on a 0-5 rubric (p. 72). This entry is restricted to the original sessions 1-3, identified by session and tool-group labels in Figures 47-55 (pp. 76-84). ChatGPT was available during writing in the original LLM arm (p. 27). Only those session-identified outputs support with_ai/yes/immediate. Pooled raw-score, z-score and assessor-comparison displays in Figures 40-46 provide measurement context, not verified phase-specific treatment estimates; assessor disagreement is not an AI-assistance effect. No overall participant-level treatment effect or uncertainty is printed. The optional session-4 outputs are outside this entry; S1-O13 records teacher-rated after-AI uniqueness and the other follow-up rating combinations are documented as omissions under the current outcome cap.

contrasts.reported: Teachers describe lower uniqueness for formulaic essays they perceived as AI-written, with exceptions for unusual examples or quotations. Topic descriptions vary: ART uniqueness is high for teachers; Brain-only uniqueness is below the teacher mean in COURAGE; LLM uniqueness is generally at or below the teacher mean in HAPPINESS and low in LOYALTY. These descriptions do not constitute an overall LLM-versus-Brain-only contrast. No exact arm difference, SD, SE or confidence interval is printed. This entry uses the session-1-3 labels in Figures 47-55; pooled assessor-comparison prose is descriptive background and is not assigned to an initial-session treatment effect.

outcomes.name: Within-group essay similarity (writer-pair composition unconfirmed)
outcomes.measure_detail: Embeddings generated using llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M; Figure 19 displays pairwise cosine similarities among all essays within each group (p. 57). Each writer produced repeated essays (pp. 23 and 28); neither the text nor caption states that same-writer pairs were excluded, and the display includes its self-similarity diagonal. Thus a measure restricted to different people is unconfirmed. Coded other as generic essay similarity, with no signed across-person diversity effect. PaCMAP group/topic plots in Figures 13-14 are related descriptive visualizations. No analyzed pair count, numeric arm-average similarity, participant-clustered SE, comparison test or confidence interval is reported. The contributing sessions and whether figure labels track original assignment or current tools are not stated. Original LLM returnees wrote without AI in session 4, and original Brain-only returnees used AI (pp. 28 and 117). Question, AI availability and timing are therefore null for this aggregate; neither exclusively assisted production nor a confirmed mixture is asserted. Contrast arm labels refer only to the displayed essay pools, and comparison_type is other. These results are not verified phase-specific randomized estimates.
outcomes.delay: Session composition of the pooled display is not stated; no production-phase or follow-up interval is assigned.

contrasts.reported: The authors describe LLM essays as more similar or homogeneous (p. 57, Fig. 19; p. 143, Discussion: NLP). No numeric group-average similarity or comparison uncertainty is printed. Whether same-writer pairs are excluded and which sessions enter each pool are unconfirmed, so the direction of a strictly across-person, phase-specific diversity effect is null; heatmap colors are not used to estimate it.

outcomes.name: Consistency of named-entity distributions (Cramer's V)
outcomes.measure_detail: Named entities were extracted and classified using llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M. Entity-frequency contingency tables were summarized using Cramer's V and averaged across topics (pp. 58-59). Figure 21 contains comparison p-values inside the raster figure, absent from the markdown. Bars have no numeric value labels, so heights are not transcribed as exact Cramer's V estimates. Entity-type frequencies in Figures 22-24 are related descriptive displays. The contributing sessions and whether figure labels track original assignment or current tools are not stated. Original LLM returnees wrote without AI in session 4, and original Brain-only returnees used AI (pp. 28 and 117). Question, AI availability and timing are therefore null for this aggregate; neither exclusively assisted production nor a confirmed mixture is asserted. Contrast arm labels refer only to the displayed essay pools, and comparison_type is other. These results are not verified phase-specific randomized estimates.
outcomes.delay: Session composition of the pooled display is not stated; no production-phase or follow-up interval is assigned.

contrasts.reported: Cramer's V is higher for LLM than Brain Only; the comparison bracket is labeled "* 0.02898". Exact arm Cramer's V values and SEs are not printed. Greater consistency is coded as lower diversity. The contributing sessions and original/current-group membership are unconfirmed.
contrasts.locator: pp. 58-59, Named Entities Recognition; p. 59, Fig. 21

contrasts.reported: Cramer's V is higher for LLM than Search Engine; the comparison bracket is labeled "** 0.00462". Exact arm Cramer's V values and SEs are not printed. Greater consistency is coded as lower diversity. The contributing sessions and original/current-group membership are unconfirmed.
contrasts.locator: pp. 58-59, Named Entities Recognition; p. 59, Fig. 21

diversity_detail.metric: Cramer's V for association/consistency in named-entity distributions, averaged by topic.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Named-entity frequencies from essays within each tool group and topic, subsequently averaged across topics; contingency-table layout and effective independent sample size are not fully specified.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Fig. 21 prints pairwise comparison p-values but does not identify the test, sampling unit or handling of repeated essays/participants. No SE or confidence interval is supplied.
diversity_detail.notes: The paper interprets larger V as greater consistency; the atlas direction is reversed. Entity frequencies and V are not counts of people. The local Llama model extracts/classifies entities; this is not an embedding measure.

outcomes.name: Repetition and overlap of n-grams across essays
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: This assisted-phase entry covers sessions 1-3 in the explicitly session-separated n-gram frequency diagrams (pp. 132-136, Figs. 79-86). Those diagrams use n-grams occurring at least 3 times in an essay. Initial LLM writers had ChatGPT available (p. 27); LLM-to-Brain session-4 results are separated in S1-O14. Earlier Figures 25-27 pool lexical frequencies by topic/group (pp. 62-65) and do not establish a phase-specific effect. Their methods specify lengths 2-5 (p. 62), whereas p. 132 calls Figure 27 order 4 and higher; that definition remains unresolved. These are group/topic essay pools, not within-person category counts.

contrasts.reported: The authors describe LLM essays as more repetitive and Brain-only essays as more variable. For CHOICES, the text says LLM and Search Engine essays remained repetitive while Brain-only essays had a highly diverse range. No overall overlap coefficient, arm SD, SE or comparative test is reported. The assisted-phase coding is restricted to the session-1-3 portions of Figures 79-86; the earlier pooled plots do not establish an initial-session effect.
contrasts.locator: pp. 62-65, Figs. 25-27; p. 133, Fig. 81 and text; p. 143, Discussion: NLP

contrasts.control_arm: Search Engine Group (web search; no LLM)
contrasts.reported: The groups have different topic-specific lexical patterns; both LLM and Search Engine show repeated phrases. No single numerical LLM-versus-Search Engine diversity contrast is reported. The assisted-phase coding is restricted to the session-1-3 portions of Figures 79-86; the earlier pooled plots do not establish an initial-session effect.

diversity_detail.metric: Frequency and overlap of repeated lemmatized n-grams.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Essay pools by tool group and topic in the explicitly separated initial sessions (Figs. 79-86); the earlier all-session figures are contextual variants, not phase-specific estimates.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Descriptive bubble/frequency and flow diagrams; no specified sampling procedure, SE or overall inferential comparison.
diversity_detail.notes: Greater repetition corresponds to lower diversity. The paper gives examples and distributions rather than an arm-level diversity score.

outcomes.name: Between-group divergence of n-gram distributions (KL divergence)
outcomes.measure_detail: Kullback-Leibler divergence between aggregated group n-gram distributions, normalized within topic, with smoothing epsilon = 1e-10; the top-left heatmap aggregates across topics (pp. 57-58, Fig. 20). This measures how group distributions differ from one another and cannot by itself rank diversity within each group. The contributing sessions and whether figure labels track original assignment or current tools are not stated. Original LLM returnees wrote without AI in session 4, and original Brain-only returnees used AI (pp. 28 and 117). Question, AI availability and timing are therefore null for this aggregate; neither exclusively assisted production nor a confirmed mixture is asserted. Contrast arm labels refer only to the displayed essay pools, and comparison_type is other. These results are not verified phase-specific randomized estimates.
outcomes.delay: Session composition of the pooled display is not stated; no production-phase or follow-up interval is assigned.

contrasts.reported: The text reports Brain-only divergence from LLM for ART, CHOICES, COURAGE, FORETHOUGHT and PHILANTHROPY; LOYALTY and HAPPINESS show less difference between LLM and Brain-only. No numeric KL cell labels, exact arm-level contrast or uncertainty are printed. Topic-specific distribution separation is not a signed within-group diversity effect. The contributing sessions and original/current-group membership are unconfirmed.
contrasts.locator: pp. 57-58, Similarities and distances; p. 58, Fig. 20

contrasts.reported: The text reports the Search Engine distribution diverging most in LOYALTY and HAPPINESS, with other patterns in other topics. The heatmaps do not establish which of these two groups has greater internal diversity. The contributing sessions and original/current-group membership are unconfirmed.
contrasts.locator: pp. 57-58, Similarities and distances; p. 58, Fig. 20

diversity_detail.metric: Kullback-Leibler divergence between group-level n-gram frequency distributions.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Aggregated n-gram distributions for pairs of tool groups, separately by topic and in an all-topic summary; not individual essay-pair distances.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No test method, numeric comparison p-value, SE or confidence interval is supplied for Fig. 20.
diversity_detail.notes: Direction is mixed because distribution separation does not identify a higher-diversity treatment arm. Normalized heatmap colors are not precise numerical estimates.

outcomes.name: Shared conceptual relationships in essay ontologies
outcomes.measure_detail: Essay ontology graphs were generated with llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M and manually checked (p. 68). The analysis counts recurring edges across different essays on the same topic within each group, matching node wording using Levenshtein distance <= 10 (p. 70, Fig. 37). The topic-level variant uses <= 20 (p. 71, Fig. 38). The contributing sessions and whether figure labels track original assignment or current tools are not stated. Original LLM returnees wrote without AI in session 4, and original Brain-only returnees used AI (pp. 28 and 117). Question, AI availability and timing are therefore null for this aggregate; neither exclusively assisted production nor a confirmed mixture is asserted. Contrast arm labels refer only to the displayed essay pools, and comparison_type is other. These results are not verified phase-specific randomized estimates.
outcomes.delay: Session composition of the pooled display is not stated; no production-phase or follow-up interval is assigned.

contrasts.reported: The authors report that LLM essays dominate repeated ontology edges, while Brain-only essays have only a handful of frequent edges and little intersection with the other tool groups. No overall overlap estimate, SD, SE or numeric inferential comparison is reported. The contributing sessions and original/current-group membership are unconfirmed.
contrasts.locator: pp. 68-71, Ontology analysis, Figs. 34 and 37-38; p. 145, Discussion: NLP

contrasts.reported: Search Engine essays are described as largely overlapping with LLM essays in reused ontology, but no clear scalar comparison of their internal diversity is given. No numeric treatment contrast or uncertainty is printed. The contributing sessions and original/current-group membership are unconfirmed.
contrasts.locator: p. 70, Fig. 37 and text; p. 145, Discussion: NLP

diversity_detail.metric: Counts of ontology edges recurring across essays after approximate matching of node labels.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Edges from each essay compared with other essays on the same topic within the same tool group; further aggregated across groups/topics.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Descriptive graph/count visualizations; no specified participant-level SE, confidence interval or quantitative comparative test.
diversity_detail.notes: More recurring relationships imply less conceptual diversity. Graph matching thresholds are tuning choices, not effect estimates. Ontology generation uses llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M; no embedding model is used for the reported Levenshtein matching.

outcomes.name: Essay length in words and sentences
outcomes.measure_detail: Raw word and sentence counts, summarized as group averages in Figure 16 (p. 55); construct elaboration, unit output. The codebook's category_count counts ideas, categories or unique ideas, not generic word/sentence totals, and automated_score denotes a creativity-scoring model. No supplied measure code fits this length measure, so measure is null rather than inventing a mapping. Words and sentences are companion length measures, not idea fluency. No SD, SE, CI or essay count accompanies the means. Figure 15 does not identify a test of these mean differences. The contributing sessions and whether figure labels track original assignment or current tools are not stated. Original LLM returnees wrote without AI in session 4, and original Brain-only returnees used AI (pp. 28 and 117). Question, AI availability and timing are therefore null for this aggregate; neither exclusively assisted production nor a confirmed mixture is asserted. Contrast arm labels refer only to the displayed essay pools, and comparison_type is other. These results are not verified phase-specific randomized estimates.
outcomes.delay: Session composition of the pooled display is not stated; no production-phase or follow-up interval is assigned.

outcomes.name: Uniqueness of unassisted essays after prior ChatGPT use
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The same blinded teacher uniqueness rubric is applied to session-4 essays produced by LLM-to-Brain returnees after ChatGPT was removed (pp. 28, 72 and 117). This is the returning subset, not a new independent sample. Figures 47-55 show session-4 points among earlier-session scores. The text does not supply a dedicated controlled after-AI uniqueness effect; comparisons across current tool groups/sessions must not be read as a randomized retention estimate. eligibility.reason: The original supervised experiment independently meets all three criteria. People were explicitly randomly assigned to ChatGPT, non-LLM web search or no tools (p. 23), with ChatGPT available during essay production (p. 27). Methods explicitly report 54 analyzed people (p. 22), and Table 1 gives 18 per original group (p. 3), meeting the 50-person threshold across all arms without treating the recruitment total as a randomized count. Blinded English teachers scored essay uniqueness on a 0-5 rubric (p. 72), and session-labeled figures include the original sessions (pp. 76-84, Figs. 47-55), so criterion 3 does not depend on uncertain pooled similarity figures. The optional session 4 reuses 18 participants and does not independently meet the sample-size or new-randomization requirements (pp. 45-46 and 117). Unresolved session composition, same-writer pair inclusion, missing precision and ancillary coding questions affect estimate extraction, not the eligibility of the original experiment.

one_line_finding: The study analyzed 54 people (p. 22); its pooled named-entity figure reports higher consistency for LLM-labeled essays than Brain Only (p = 0.02898) or Search Engine (p = 0.00462), but the contributing sessions and test are unspecified (p. 59, Fig. 21).
open_questions: Exact revision date/arXiv version of the saved preprint is not established: publication prose says June 2025, but reference 129 was retrieved December 12, 2025 (pp. 151, 154, 166).

Numbers randomized, assignment-stage arm counts, timing/reason for excluding the completed case, and arm-specific losses are missing; educational-status totals also differ from the explicit analyzed denominator (p. 22).
The participant-facing ChatGPT model/version is not stated in the intervention description (pp. 23, 27).
Which sessions and original/current tool groups contribute to each pooled NLP/rating display, and are same-writer pairs excluded from within-group semantic similarity (pp. 52-59, 73-84)?
Which test and independent sampling units produced the Figure 21 p-values, and what are the exact Cramer's V values and participant-level uncertainty (pp. 58-59)?

The uniqueness-specific before/after comparison proposed by A cannot be confirmed: Table 1 does not identify that metric or comparator, and no matched uniqueness estimate is printed (pp. 3-4, 76, 122).

PaCMAP change has no established signed creativity interpretation; Figure 12 additionally shows Search Engine transitions despite the stated absence of a Search Engine fourth session (pp. 4, 28, 52-53, 117).

Figure 15 does not specify the null/test behind its group-labeled p-values; prose alternates between word length and essay word counts. Figure 16 also does not support the Table 1 claim that Brain-only essays were shortest (pp. 4, 55).

N-gram specifications differ between the lengths 2-5 description and the later order-4-and-higher description; the Figure 83 caption and its prose also identify different repeated phrases (pp. 62, 132, 134).
How do Vocabulary/Grammar in the methods map to Language and Style/Accuracy in the plots (pp. 72-76)?
For reference-essay cosine distance, how does the prose/caption comparison to a generated reference correspond to the all-pairs expression in equation (1) (p. 56)?

Participant-linked essay scores, repeated-measure identifiers and analysis code are needed for independent effect/uncertainty extraction; the PDF identifies a project website, not explicit data/code repositories (p. 5; pp. 52-84; appendices pp. 167-216).

Figure 16 word/sentence counts have no matching measure code in the current codebook; measure is null rather than category_count or automated_score (p. 55; creativity-codebook.md, section 6). This is a coding-vocabulary issue, not missing evidence of output scoring.
notes: Finalized on 2026-10-09. Independently read the entire saved markdown in consecutive chunks (401,907 characters, 5,477 lines), including all references and Appendices A-BC. Checked relevant PDF pages with PyMuPDF text extraction and recovered Table 1 with find_tables. Inspected Figures 12, 15, 16, 18, 19, 21, 40-41, 51 and 54 by rendering PDF regions in memory; no image files were created. The recorded Figure 15 p-value labels, Figure 16 means, Figure 18 distances and Figure 21 p-values match the PDF. No effect sizes, uncertainties, essay/pair counts or unlabeled plot heights were calculated. PDF page numbers are used throughout. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as historical provenance, including its two unresolved differences; current final decisions and coding supersede its earlier measure mapping and retention of 17 outcomes. Current form-spec.md rule 7 limits the array to 15 main outcomes. The retained set prioritizes teacher and AI uniqueness, group-level language/concept patterns, essay quality, reported length means, and the expressly discussed after-AI uniqueness and lexical results. No output outcome is explicitly named primary or preregistered. Stable outcome IDs are preserved; S1-O15 and S1-O17 are omitted from the array because they are ancillary distance measures without an established creativity direction. Former S1-O15 (pp. 52-53, Fig. 12) is same-writer, same-topic PaCMAP change after a tool switch, averaged per participant/topic; it is not across-person diversity. It has no printed numeric bar labels, comparative p-value, SE or CI. Search Engine transitions in that figure conflict with the stated absence of a Search Engine session 4 (p. 4) and need clarification. Former S1-O17 (pp. 55-56, Figs. 17-18) compares participant essays with a generated reference: printed mean cosine distances are LLM 0.48301, Search Engine 0.54371, Brain Only 0.48579, without SD, SE or CI. Its equation averages unique vector pairs while the prose/caption describe a reference comparison. Session composition is unspecified; these numbers are neither verified initial-session treatment effects nor a demonstrated creativity/diversity ranking. Other source-confirmed measures omitted under the same cap are AI-judge Language and Style; teacher and AI Accuracy (pp. 72-75, Figs. 40-45); AI-rated after-AI uniqueness and teacher/AI after-AI content, language/style and structure/organization (pp. 76-84, Figs. 47-55, especially blue session-4 crosses in Figs. 51 and 54); rubric length scores without a distinct reported summary; and Figure 15's ambiguous length-dispersion result. All omitted LLM-to-Brain ratings would be after_ai/no/delayed if extracted separately, not with_ai; they have no printed controlled retention contrast. Accuracy is essay quality, not a convergent creativity test; the mapping of Vocabulary/Grammar to the plotted labels is unspecified. Figure 15 (p. 55) prints group-labeled p-values LLM 0.39, Search Engine 0.02, Brain Only 0.49. Its null/test is unspecified and the prose alternates between word length and essay word count. These are not variances or pairwise treatment-comparison p-values and must not be attached to Figure 16 mean differences. The omission challenges are rejected only as demands for additional coded rows under the current cap; the existence of these output measures is confirmed. Null question/availability/timing fields for pooled outcomes denote unconfirmed attribution, not a known mixed phase and not an irrelevant outcome. Their contrast labels reproduce figure labels, and comparison_type other prevents treating them as verified initial-assignment contrasts. Initial-session rating entries use session-labeled Figures 47-55; the assisted n-gram entry uses the initial-session portions of Figures 79-86. S1-O2 is retained as generic output similarity (other), with no certified cross-writer-only measure or signed diversity effect. S1-O12 measure is null because the supplied measure vocabulary does not include raw length counts. Figure 16 means remain descriptive figure_only results because no means-only statistics code is supplied. Figure 21 p-values are not effect sizes; sampling/testing and participant-level precision remain unspecified. KL distribution separation cannot rank internal group diversity. Known similarity, named-entity consistency and repeated-concept directions are described with their limits; no_clear_difference means insufficient comparative evidence, not equivalence. The five arm entries reuse people and must not be summed: the analyzed original sample is 54, and the session-4 returnees are a subset. A procedural pilot on p. 23 has no separate reported randomized creative-output results. No concurrent never-AI unassisted session-4 control or clean causal after-AI estimate is established. General high follow-up scores do not establish a matched uniqueness improvement. EEG, recall/quoting, prompt recognition, ownership, satisfaction, interview/prompt classifications, AI-authorship detection and energy estimates are excluded as not creativity/diversity scored on the produced essays. The included appendices supply no additional essay-outcome precision. No explicit data/code repository is identified in the PDF; the project website remains only a project link. Only forms/c416.json is written.

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: Exact revision date/arXiv version of the saved preprint is not established: publication prose says June 2025, but reference 129 was retrieved December 12, 2025 (pp. 151, 154, 166). Identification of the exact revision of the saved PDF would settle the conflicting date evidence.

open_questions[1]: Numbers randomized, assignment-stage arm counts, timing/reason for excluding the completed case, and arm-specific losses are missing; educational-status totals also differ from the explicit analyzed denominator (p. 22). A participant-flow account and assignment-stage denominators would settle these discrepancies; the explicit 54 analyzed people already meets criterion 2.

open_questions[2]: The participant-facing ChatGPT model/version is not stated in the intervention description (pp. 23, 27). The intervention account/model record would identify the participant-facing ChatGPT version.

open_questions[3]: Which sessions and original/current tool groups contribute to each pooled NLP/rating display, and are same-writer pairs excluded from within-group semantic similarity (pp. 52-59, 73-84)? Participant/session identifiers and analysis code would identify each pooled figure composition and exclusion of same-writer pairs; initial-session teacher uniqueness already establishes criterion 3.

open_questions[4]: Which test and independent sampling units produced the Figure 21 p-values, and what are the exact Cramer's V values and participant-level uncertainty (pp. 58-59)? The NER contingency tables, participant identifiers and test code would establish the printed test, exact values and independent-unit precision.

open_questions[5]: The uniqueness-specific before/after comparison proposed by A cannot be confirmed: Table 1 does not identify that metric or comparator, and no matched uniqueness estimate is printed (pp. 3-4, 76, 122). A uniqueness-specific comparator for Table 1 and a matched score analysis are needed; no matched improvement is currently recorded.

open_questions[6]: PaCMAP change has no established signed creativity interpretation; Figure 12 additionally shows Search Engine transitions despite the stated absence of a Search Engine fourth session (pp. 4, 28, 52-53, 117). The authors must explain the Search Engine transitions in Figure 12. A signed creativity interpretation is not established by content-change distance, and that ancillary outcome is now documented only in notes.

open_questions[7]: Figure 15 does not specify the null/test behind its group-labeled p-values; prose alternates between word length and essay word counts. Figure 16 also does not support the Table 1 claim that Brain-only essays were shortest (pp. 4, 55). The Figure 15 outcome definition, null and test, and the Table 1 versus Figure 16 length inconsistency require clarification.

open_questions[8]: N-gram specifications differ between the lengths 2-5 description and the later order-4-and-higher description; the Figure 83 caption and its prose also identify different repeated phrases (pp. 62, 132, 134). N-gram extraction code and source essay/session records would settle the specifications and repeated-phrase discrepancy.

open_questions[9]: How do Vocabulary/Grammar in the methods map to Language and Style/Accuracy in the plots (pp. 72-76)? The grading rubric and mapping to displayed metric names would settle this terminology issue.

open_questions[10]: For reference-essay cosine distance, how does the prose/caption comparison to a generated reference correspond to the all-pairs expression in equation (1) (p. 56)? The implementation and reference/participant vector identifiers would settle equation (1) versus the Figure 18 prose; this ancillary outcome is documented only in notes.

open_questions[11]: Participant-linked essay scores, repeated-measure identifiers and analysis code are needed for independent effect/uncertainty extraction; the PDF identifies a project website, not explicit data/code repositories (p. 5; pp. 52-84; appendices pp. 167-216). Participant-linked scores and reproducible analysis code would permit extraction of independent-unit uncertainty; no such repository is identified in the saved PDF.

open_questions[12]: Figure 16 word/sentence counts have no matching measure code in the current codebook; measure is null rather than category_count or automated_score (p. 55; creativity-codebook.md, section 6). This is a coding-vocabulary issue, not missing evidence of output scoring. The source already establishes raw word/sentence counting. Retaining measure=null avoids an unsupported vocabulary mapping; only an editorial codebook decision could supply a new label.

reconciliation.differences[6], before/after teacher uniqueness: still unconfirmed because Table 1 does not identify a uniqueness-specific metric/comparator. A clarification of that claim and matched participant scores would settle it; it is not needed for original-study eligibility.

reconciliation.differences[8], signed PaCMAP creativity direction: no further source is needed for the screening decision. Figure 12 defines content/structure change, which does not establish a signed creativity effect. The ancillary outcome is omitted from the main-15 array and described in notes without a creativity direction. The separate Search Engine transition inconsistency remains an authors item above.
